Disappointed the open-source release didn't include commit history: they wanted to branch from ~5 years ago, when Warp was just a terminal, and strip out 'all the AI and cloud shit' to get a nice terminal with some neat features.

Has lived in a terminal for 30+ years and wanted to try Warp immediately, but the login requirement put them off, so they never tried it. They also criticize heavy telemetry as a privacy nightmare: 'a terminal that is not designed for users.'
'I really like Warp. It's a lot nicer to be able to visualize what I'm doing in the terminal.' They note the AI features only activate if you log in.
Calls Warp 'a masterclass in how to have a great product statement, very nice UI and completely ruin it with greed, closed-source, and by not listening to your customers.'

User got an unexpected LLM suggestion for fixing a syntax error after running a test. They discovered Warp's Active AI (Prompt Suggestions/Next Command) sends terminal errors, inputs and outputs to LLMs proactively, without explicit consent. Called it an enormous breach of trust and removed Warp despite enjoying it.

Uninstalled after finding basic terminal functions broken. Warp hijacks 'clear', so 'clear && cmd' doesn't work as in other terminals. A long-open bug report suggested Warp had no interest in fixing it.

Another user points out Prompt Suggestions and Next Command can be disabled in settings. A reply says they should be disabled by default or shown with a big warning, since they often set secret tokens as env variables.
Current Warp user finds the history/context-aware 'autocomplete-on-meth' nice, but doesn't use the new agentic features and is looking for a replacement.
'I'm a Warp fanboy. Claude Code has it beat for writing software, but Warp is magic for linux sys admin.' They SSH into a home server and no longer switch to a browser to Google things.
Self-described noob who values privacy elsewhere finds Warp super powerful. For example, they have it find old unused files, examine them and suggest whether they can be deleted.
Had high hopes for Warp before launch, but it 'slowly enshittified'; switched to Ghostty.

Tried Warp, was asked to sign in, and uninstalled faster than any program ever; sticking with iTerm. They suggest it would have been better to gate only the account-requiring features behind login rather than block even a local zsh prompt.
'Warp is great - I use it as my daily terminal.' Best features: being able to edit commands, output chunked into blocks, and AI-generated commands at your fingertips.
Warp has been their daily driver for months, even after trying Rio, Ghostty and WezTerm. Favorite feature is the notification when a long-running command finishes.
Deal breaker: objects to sending shell input to a third party, opt-out telemetry, and a 'trust us' privacy policy. Worries users will be left with nothing if the VC-funded startup shuts down.

Warp has been 'horribly broken' for weeks: a consistent issue writing files (multiple GitHub issues), UI glitches, and code indexing and the file/diff explorer unusable over WSL or SSH. Liked it a lot before, but now 'practically unusable.'
Pro user (under 1000 credits/month) has noticed a real drop in quality over the past month, including random failures and agents stopping.
Ghostty user used to consider Warp a 'shitty AI powered terminal' until seeing a demo. Now sees it as a fair AI agent application with good CLI integration and some notebook features.
Found Warp interesting but 'honestly overwhelming' when simply reaching for a terminal; went back to Terminal.app.

Finds nearly everything about Warp's terminal experience better than iTerm, especially treating the terminal like a text file with modern mouse/text editing. Turned off all AI features. Has issues SSHing into one machine; works around it by using 'command ssh' for that host.
